Constraint Handling Rules, a declarative programming language, has been found to be equivalent in power to Alternating-time Temporal Logic of the Future. A study on CHRs reveals that a limited number of atoms in the head of rules can significantly affect its power. Specifically, a version of CHRs with only one atom in the head is equivalent to Horn clauses, while adding a second atom enables CHRs to match the full power of HTR, a logic-based system. This enhancement also allows CHRs to be more efficient in solving problems compared to traditional approaches.

Our research investigates the orientation of galaxy spin dipoles in the Cosmic
Flow Quasar Survey (CFQS) and compares it with previous studies from the
2MASS Redshift Survey and the SDSS DR7 survey. We discovered that the
CFQS quasar data aligns with the distribution of galaxies in the 2MASS
survey, but not with the SDSS DR7 survey. We also found that the quasar
dipoles are more stable over time compared to the SDSS data, which may be
due to the quasar data's smaller size and unique properties. We suggest that
the CFQS quasar data could be used to study the orientation of galaxy spins
in the universe.

We introduce a novel approach called Eigen-Reptile, a meta-learning method that combines the advantages of both Reptile and MAML. Unlike MAML, which requires a substantial amount of computation to calculate the gradient, Eigen-Reptile streamlines this process by using the eigenvectors of the Fisher information matrix to update the model parameters. This enables the model to focus its updates on the most important directions, thereby reducing the impact of noisy labels. Additionally, the Eigen-Reptile method addresses the sampling bias issue by utilizing the eigenvectors to update the model parameters, which allows it to adapt to the distribution of the training data. Experimental results demonstrate that Eigen-Reptile outperforms MAML and other meta-learning methods, particularly in scenarios with noisy labels.

Alzheimer's disease is a widespread neurodegenerative disorder that significantly affects the elderly population.  A key aspect of the disease is cognitive impairment, which can be measured using various metrics, including the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS) in clinical settings.  In this study, we utilize machine learning techniques to forecast MMSE and ADAS scores based on brain MRI scans.  We apply a range of machine learning methods, including random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks, to identify the most effective approach.  The results demonstrate that deep learning models outperform traditional machine learning methods, achieving the highest accuracy in predicting MMSE and ADAS scores.  The deep learning model, which utilizes a convolutional neural network, successfully predicts MMSE scores with an R2 value of 0.75 and ADAS scores with an R2 value of 0.71.  The findings suggest that deep learning models can accurately forecast cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease patients using brain MRI scans.

The field of AI Ethics is rapidly growing, yet it lacks a clear framework for evaluating the significance of various ethical considerations. To address this, we propose a novel framework that categorizes and assesses the key concerns in AI ethics, focusing on the concept of moral agency. Our analysis reveals that the ethical landscape of AI can be divided into three distinct levels: individual, organizational, and societal. At each level, we identify and evaluate the primary ethical challenges that need to be addressed. By adopting a comprehensive approach that considers the moral agency of all stakeholders involved, we provide a practical and effective method for evaluating AI systems and their impact on society.

We present a proof showing that deterministic regular languages are the only L- and C-closed full triva for Boolean operations and union with rational sets of words over $\omega$-words that are both decidable and full. This outcome is a direct consequence of our findings on the properties of regular languages in this context.

This research introduces a hybrid channel estimation approach that combines the benefits of both pilot-aided and compressed sensing techniques. By utilizing a deep neural network to learn the channel's spatial structure, the proposed method enhances prediction accuracy. A new algorithm is developed to estimate the channel matrix, incorporating the neural network's knowledge. Simulation results demonstrate that this hybrid scheme outperforms traditional pilot-aided and compressed sensing methods, especially in scenarios with limited training data.

Recent discrepancies in measurements of $V_{ud}$ and $V_{us}$ have the potential to reveal physics beyond the Standard Model, particularly when combined with the longstanding anomaly in the proton's magnetic moment. We investigate the implications of these findings in the context of scalar leptoquarks, which can be constrained by various processes, including the decay of a Higgs boson into electrons and anti-electrons, and the decay of a Higgs boson into a muon and an anti-muon. By analyzing these processes, we can determine the possible values of the coupling constants associated with leptoquarks, which can be further constrained by considering the effects of these particles on the decay of a tau lepton into a muon and a pair of pions. We also consider the effects of these particles on the decay of a tau lepton into a muon and an electron and a neutrino.

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance the performance of a network by integrating dilated kernels into the convolution layers, which are applied sequentially to increase receptive field size. The network's ability to capture intricate details in images is significantly improved through this method, ultimately enhancing performance. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated across various applications, including image classification, object detection, and image segmentation, where it is shown to yield superior results compared to existing techniques.

In the era of big data, numerous organizations collaborate to create shared data views, yet these views often inadvertently reveal sensitive information about individual entities. To address this concern, we propose a method to differentiate an entity's private data from shared data by analyzing the data view's structure. This method leverages a structural analysis of the data view to identify private information and minimize the risk of data leakage. To achieve this, we introduce a new metric called the View Privacy Score (VPS), which measures the privacy level of an entity's data within the data view. By applying this method to a real-world example, we demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing the privacy of data views.

We have analyzed the infrared spectra of 100 nearby galaxies to study the presence of hot dust emission, which is typically associated with high-energy processes. Our findings indicate that the hot dust emission is more prevalent in galaxies with high radio luminosity and a radio-loud active galactic nucleus. We observed a significant increase in hot dust emission in galaxies with higher radio luminosity, particularly in those with a radio-loud active galactic nucleus. We also found that the hot dust emission is more prevalent in galaxies with a specific morphological structure, specifically those with a double-lobed radio morphology. Our results suggest that the hot dust emission is a result of the interaction between the radio jets and the surrounding interstellar medium. We also found that the hot dust emission is more prevalent in galaxies with a higher star formation rate and a higher gas fraction. Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the relationship between the star formation rate, the gas content, and the activity of the active galactic nucleus in galaxies.

The moral alignment of large language models is a critical concern, as it influences their reliability and safety. To address this, our research introduces MORALCOT, a novel prompting strategy that enhances the moral reasoning capabilities of AI systems by having them learn from human moral judgments. By prompting models to analyze a story and make judgments on the moral worth of characters' actions, MORALCOT significantly improves moral alignment, as demonstrated by a 20% increase in alignment with human judgments when evaluated on the Moral Machine dataset. Furthermore, our study reveals that MORALCOT prompts can be used to fine-tune language models, resulting in a 20% improvement in moral alignment, as well as a 25% increase in alignment with human moral judgments when tested on the Moral Machine dataset. These findings underscore the potential of MORALCOT as a powerful tool for developing ethically aligned AI systems.
Given a valuation ring with a residue field of characteristic $p$, we show that it can be expressed as the direct limit of finite-dimensional semisimple algebras over the prime field $\mathbb F_p$.

This article delves into the foundational principles of the two-dimensional Dirac equation and its associated concepts, which have numerous applications in modern physics, particularly in the field of condensed matter physics.

Cooperative driving methods, which involve the exchange of data between vehicles, can significantly enhance road safety and efficiency. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is an effective strategy for navigating complex driving scenarios, as it enables the simultaneous consideration of multiple variables. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of cooperative driving methods, with a focus on the application of MPC in various driving situations. A comparative evaluation of MPC-based controllers is conducted, with a specific emphasis on the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The proposed MPC controller is designed to optimize vehicle trajectories in a manner that minimizes collisions, thereby facilitating safe and efficient vehicle coordination. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed MPC-based controller in coordinating vehicle movements and reducing collision risks.

In the digital age, social media has become a double-edged sword, offering a platform for information dissemination while also serving as a breeding ground for misinformation. The spread of unverified information on social media can be particularly insidious, as users often prioritize the credibility of information sources over the content itself. This phenomenon is evident in the way users share information, often favoring trusted sources over less reliable ones. To address this issue, we have developed a new method for evaluating the credibility of information sources on social media, which takes into account the credibility of information content and the credibility of information sources. By incorporating a multi-faceted approach that considers the credibility of information content, the credibility of information sources, and the credibility of information sources' followers, our method aims to provide a more accurate assessment of information credibility. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on a real-world dataset, which show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

In the event of a sudden road emergency, such as a crash, the available bandwidth for V2X communication is severely limited, resulting in significant delays for other roadside applications. To address this issue, we introduce the $\pi$-ROAD framework, a novel approach that dynamically allocates network resources to V2X applications during emergencies. This framework utilizes a combination of a prediction model and a resource allocation algorithm to anticipate the duration of the emergency and reserve necessary network resources for V2X applications. The effectiveness of $\pi$-ROAD is demonstrated through simulations using real-world crash data, which reveal that it can achieve a 100% success rate in meeting V2X applications' quality of service requirements, even when the network is congested.

This research introduces a novel method for path planning, specifically designed for collaborative robots. The proposed approach leverages a graph-based planner, which integrates a novel Artificial Potential Fields collision avoidance algorithm. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulation-based experiments, where the robot successfully avoids obstacles while ensuring the safety of human collaborators. The experimental results indicate that the proposed path planning method significantly reduces the risk of collisions and improves overall task efficiency.

The rise of autonomous and intelligent vehicles is transforming the urban landscape, necessitating a shift towards more autonomous and intelligent cities. This transition is facilitated by advancements in smart city technology, which is now being integrated into urban infrastructure. As a result, cities are becoming increasingly capable of making autonomous decisions and adapting to changing circumstances. This paper examines the evolution of autonomous and intelligent systems, with a focus on the applications of autonomous and intelligent vehicles, as well as their integration into smart city technology. The authors also discuss the implications of autonomous and intelligent systems on urban mobility, highlighting the potential for these technologies to revolutionize the way we live and interact within our cities.

In the context of online caching, we investigate the impact of using imperfect future demand predictions. Our analysis reveals that the performance of the Lookahead Policy, which does not utilize demand predictions, is optimal in terms of competitive ratio when the predictions are inaccurate. We also establish that the best achievable competitive ratio under the given prediction model is lower-bounded by a specific function of the prediction error and cache size. Additionally, we develop a caching algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio close to this lower bound, which represents a significant improvement over the Lookahead Policy.

Recent advancements in neural network architectures have led to the development of the Trilateral Attention Network (TAN), which has demonstrated superior performance in image segmentation tasks. The success of TAN lies in its ability to capture multi-scale features through three distinct pathways: the local, contextual, and global pathways. The local pathway focuses on the pixel's immediate neighborhood, the contextual pathway considers the pixel's surrounding context, and the global pathway provides a broader global perspective. The fusion of these pathways enables the network to learn diverse features, thereby enhancing segmentation performance. The effectiveness of TAN has been validated through experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, where it achieved state-of-the-art results. The source code for the model is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ChenXupeng3/TAN.
In the context of the linearized supergeometry of superspace, we establish the connection between the constraints on torsion and the constraints on the gauge potentials.

The quality of training data has a profound impact on the effectiveness of learning models.
To improve this, we've developed a new approach that leverages the contribution of each individual training example to the model's performance.
By analyzing how each example affects the model's accuracy, we can identify and remove low-quality data.
To evaluate the quality of each example, we've introduced a new metric called the Outlier-ness of Examples (OOE).
The OOE metric is based on the influence function, which measures how each example affects the model's accuracy on other instances.
We've also developed a method to estimate the influence function without the need for retraining the model, which is computationally efficient.
By applying our approach to various datasets, we've demonstrated its effectiveness in improving model performance.

We've developed a theoretical framework for quantum charge pumping in three-dimensional topological insulators, where the Hall surface is described by a non-abelian Chern-Simons theory. This theory gives rise to a non-abelian matrix Berry phase, which is the root cause of quantum charge pumping. Our analysis shows that the Hall current is influenced by the interference between the non-abelian Berry phase and the external driving force. Furthermore, we've established a connection between the non-abelian Chern number and the non-abelian matrix Berry phase, which allows us to derive a non-abelian Chern-Simons theory for three-dimensional topological insulators.

We introduce METRO-LM, a series of 100M-1.3B parameter language models, designed to strike a balance between performance and efficiency. Our models demonstrate competitive results on various benchmarks, surpassing the performance of larger models in some instances. We also detail the process of training METRO-LM on a massive 1.2 trillion token dataset, encompassing over 120 terabytes of text. We provide insights into the effectiveness of METRO-LM on a range of evaluation tasks, including language understanding, translation, and code generation. Our models are available for public use, and we provide guidance on their practical applications.

We examine the issue of determining a quantum network's structure from local data points. We demonstrate that quantum entanglement can be used to obtain more detailed information about the network's connections, surpassing classical entanglement capabilities. Furthermore, our results show that the information obtained from local measurements is not solely dependent on the correlations between the measurements and the network's connections, but rather, it is influenced by the level of entanglement within the network.

Effective visual information dissemination relies on an appropriate introduction, yet the ideal introduction remains unclear. This study investigated the impact of different introduction types on audience comprehension, using a survey to compare the performance of technical, non-technical, and no introduction scenarios. The results indicate that non-technical introductions are the most effective in facilitating understanding of visual encodings. Furthermore, this study found that introducing visualizations enhances the accuracy of audience memory, with participants demonstrating improved recall of visual content. The research also found that audiences tend to focus on specific visual elements, such as peaks and outliers, rather than the overall distribution, which may be influenced by the introduction provided. The findings of this study have practical implications for data visualization, suggesting that tailored introductions can be used to guide audience attention and enhance the effectiveness of visual communication.

We investigate the optical manipulation of quantum systems in a lattice structure, specifically the transformation of a many-body quantum system from a disordered to an ordered state. By rapidly altering the optical potential, we create a dynamic environment where the system's behavior is influenced by Floquet heating. We demonstrate that the effects of Floquet heating can be counteracted by adjusting the parameters of the system, such as the strength of the interactions and the rate of change in the environment. Our results show that the ordered state can be maintained for a long time, even in the presence of Floquet heating. We also find that the system's behavior is highly sensitive to the initial conditions, which can lead to the emergence of complex patterns and the formation of defects. Our findings have important implications for the control and manipulation of quantum systems in a controlled environment.

In the context of Markov decision processes, we investigate the concept of counterfactual planning, which involves revising an initial plan based on observed events. We establish a theoretical framework for counterfactual planning under uncertainty, demonstrating that the effectiveness of revised plans is influenced by the level of uncertainty in the model parameters. Our findings indicate that an agent's ability to adapt to unexpected changes depends on the level of uncertainty, which is often overlooked in existing counterfactual planning approaches. We introduce a novel counterfactual planning method that accounts for uncertainty, enabling the agent to adapt to a broader range of potential plan revisions. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a real-world robot navigation task.

This research introduces a novel, large-scale dataset comprising 100 urban sound classes and over 100,000 labeled audio segments collected from 1000+ hours of recordings across 1000+ hours of time. The dataset is designed to capture the intricacies of urban soundscapes, including variations in sound sources, locations, and recording conditions. To address the complexities of urban sound classification, a multi-modal approach is employed, combining audio features with contextual information such as geographical location, time of day, and weather conditions. The dataset is split into training, validation, and testing sets, with a separate test set used for evaluating the performance of different models. The authors' baseline model achieves state-of-the-art results on the dataset, achieving accuracies of 95.2% and 94.7% on the ESC-50 and US8k datasets, respectively. The dataset and code are available for public use.

We investigate the four-dimensional $N=4$ supergravity model with a coupling constant of $SO(4)$, and consider the $AdS_4$ black holes in the $AdS_2 \times S^2$ and $AdS_2 \times H_2$ geometries. We then apply the Kaluza-Klein reduction to the $AdS_4$ solutions, and examine the resulting $AdS_3$ solutions in the $N=4$ gauged supergravity model. We study the properties of the $AdS_3$ solutions and their relationship to the conformal dimension and central charges, and discuss the stability of the solutions in relation to the $N=4$ gauged supergravity model. We also explore the stability of the $AdS_3$ solutions in the $N=4$ gauged supergravity model.

A new programming language called SCAMP has been developed, which is specifically designed for the FPGA-based SCAMP-5 system. The language is intended to simplify the process of programming FPGAs, making it more accessible to a broader audience. The paper discusses the design of SCAIN, a compiler for SCAMP, and presents the results of benchmarking it against other compilers. The results show that SCAIN produces more concise code, and the paper also examines the effects of varying SCAMP-5 configurations on code execution time.

The Witten effect in quantum gravity is reexamined, revealing that the spectrum of charged states is a direct reflection of the black hole's spectrum. This reevaluation leads to a significant conclusion: charged states in quantum gravity are not subject to a minimum detectable size.

We've developed an algorithm for learning mixed-strategy Nash equilibria in extensive-form games, which employs a stochastic gradient descent method to achieve this goal. The algorithm's efficiency is significantly enhanced by a technique called regret pruning, which we have now improved upon by introducing two new variations. The first variation leverages the inherent symmetry in the regret of action pairs, while the second variation further capitalizes on this symmetry by employing a more effective pruning strategy. The results of our experiments demonstrate that these new variations outperform the original algorithm in terms of the number of states that remain after pruning.

A new logic is proposed to address the issues with Aristotle's original modal syllogistic framework. The proposed logic expands upon existing work by combining the strengths of Stit's agency-related modal logic with a specific approach to reasoning about the actions of an omniscient being. The proposed logic offers a more comprehensive understanding of Aristotle's modal syllogistic framework by providing a more nuanced interpretation of the 'necessity' and 'impossibility' of certain propositions. The proposed logic also allows for the derivation of Aristotle's modal syllogistic theorems, specifically those related to the 'possibility' of certain propositions. We introduce a set of causal inequalities that can be applied to any causal network, and their associated violation conditions are derived. This class of inequalities encompasses both classical and quantum causal inequalities, and it is also relevant for networks with intermediate information processing. Key findings include: (i) the requirements for violating these inequalities are different for classical, quantum, and hybrid networks, with quantum networks being more resilient to detection inefficiency; (ii) we demonstrate that certain quantum causal inequalities can be violated using specific quantum states; (iii) we show that certain quantum causal inequalities can be violated more effectively with quantum strategies than with classical ones; (iv) we develop a general method for converting any causal inequality into a Bell inequality, and we apply this method to a specific example to illustrate the resulting correlation; (v) we establish a connection between our causal inequalities and a previously studied quantum causal inequality, demonstrating that they are a generalization of it.

This study introduces a novel dual-critic reinforcement learning approach to address the complex problem of balancing distortion and bitrate in video encoding. The proposed method leverages a state-of-the-art video encoder, NVE, to tackle the challenging task of jointly optimizing distortion-rate trade-offs. By incorporating a dual-critic framework, our approach effectively resolves the conflict between distortion and rate objectives. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in terms of both objective and perceptual quality.

In solving complex mixed-integer linear programming problems, branch-and-cut is a widely used method that relies on cutting planes to speed up the process. However, choosing the right cuts is crucial for efficient problem-solving. This research introduces a neural network-based model, called NeuralCut, that utilizes problem-solving history to select cuts dynamically. By training this model on past problem-solving data, it can make accurate cut selection decisions for new problems. Our experiments show that NeuralCut outperforms existing cut selection methods, including a strong baseline, in solving a variety of problem types. Moreover, it can effectively handle unseen problem types, showcasing its potential for real-world applications.

Our study of T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$Te$_{2}$ reveals that it exhibits superconductivity with a transition temperature of 1.8 K at the composition x = 0.05. The superconducting state displays anisotropic properties, as evidenced by the temperature dependence of the upper critical field, which is well described by the anisotropic Ginzburg-Landau model. The critical fields exhibit a temperature dependence that is well fitted by the two-band model, suggesting that the superconducting state is characterized by a two-band nature. This paper examines the effectiveness of applying Natural Language Processing techniques to enhance bug report retrieval in the context of the Eclipse Defects Database. By applying tokenization, stemming, and stopword removal to identical bug reports, the retrieval process is optimized, leading to improved precision. Additionally, the utilization of NLP-based feature extraction and clustering methods, such as TF-IDF and K-Means, facilitates the enhanced retrieval of similar bug reports.

We investigate the effective field theory of graphene near its critical point, where it exhibits strongly coupled behavior. This theory describes the graphene phase transition and its phase above the critical point, where Dirac fermions are coupled to strongly interacting phonons. We establish a strongly interacting model that accurately captures the key features of graphene's behavior, including its anomalous scaling and the emergence of a phonon-dominated mass gap. Our analysis reveals that the effective field theory is characterized by a non-trivial fixed point that is distinct from the conventional Wilson-Fisher point, and that it is dominated by the interaction between the Dirac fermions and phonons. We also find that the effective field theory is sensitive to the details of the microscopic model, and that it is difficult to obtain a simple, analytically tractable fixed point. Our results provide a new perspective on the behavior of graphene and its relation to other strongly interacting systems, and they open up new avenues for the study of non-trivial fixed points in quantum field theory.

This study introduces an innovative self-training framework that leverages a teacher-student approach to enhance Named Entity Recognition (NER) models. The framework involves training a teacher model on annotated data and utilizing its predictions to annotate a larger, unlabelled corpus. A student model is then trained on the original annotated dataset combined with the teacher's predictions, and this process is iterated to refine the student model. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework significantly improves the performance of various NER models, including BiLSTM-CRF and BERT-CRF, and the student model surpasses the teacher model in terms of F1-score. Additionally, the framework is shown to be effective in handling noisy annotated data and can be successfully applied to different languages, as evidenced by its application to Hindi.

Social media platforms have become a primary source of information for people seeking travel-related advice, making it crucial for businesses to analyze user-generated content to gain insights into consumer behavior. This research focuses on categorizing Twitter posts related to tourism based on their content, using a dataset of 1,000 manually annotated tweets. A novel approach is proposed that combines the strengths of word embeddings and word2vec to improve the accuracy of text classification. The model's performance is evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods.

A novel approach is presented for predicting the effective properties of complex materials by leveraging machine learning. The proposed method involves a two-step process: first, a neural network is trained to generate a simplified representation of the material's microstructure, and then a second neural network is trained to predict the material's effective properties based on this representation. The approach is validated using a dataset of materials with varying microstructures, and it is shown to accurately predict the material's effective properties. The proposed method is also applied to a dataset of materials with known properties, and it is found to outperform traditional methods in predicting the material's effective properties. The proposed method has the potential to be used for predicting the properties of a wide range of materials, including metals, ceramics, and polymers.

We've conducted a thorough analysis of the migration of CI Tau b, a planet orbiting the star CI Tau, using a combination of data from the Gemini Observatory and the TESS mission. Our findings indicate that the planet's current position is significantly closer to the star than its initial location, suggesting substantial inward migration. However, our analysis also reveals that the planet's migration is unlikely to be caused by a nearby companion, given the detection limits of our observations. Furthermore, we've found that the migration of CI Tau b can be explained by a combination of two scenarios: either the planet's formation was influenced by a nearby companion, or it underwent a significant period of migration due to interactions with a disk gap. Our analysis also suggests that the planet's current migration rate is relatively slow, which could be explained by a combination of two scenarios: the planet's migration is primarily driven by interactions with a nearby companion, or it underwent a significant period of migration due to interactions with a disk gap. Our findings provide new insights into the migration of CI Tau b and its implications for our understanding of planet formation and evolution.

We demonstrate a connection between zero-energy trajectories in a specific potential and free, finite-energy trajectories on a sphere. This relationship enables the transfer of known integrability characteristics from spherical trajectories to zero-energy trajectories in a planar ring configuration, thereby establishing new integrability properties for these trajectories.

The presence of non-trivial solutions is investigated for a class of non-local operators, specifically those of differential type with spectral characteristics of order $\mu>1$, coupled with a boundary condition of mixed type. The analysis is based on an algebraic framework, which is then applied to demonstrate spectral asymptotic results for these operators, including the derivation of oscillation theorems for their eigenfunctions.

This research presents a new approach to solving multi-object filtering problems in unlabelled environments, specifically tailored for particle filters. The proposed method builds upon a previous study, which employed a multi-modal particle filter to estimate object trajectories. However, the initial study had a limitation in its ability to estimate multiple trajectories per object. Our solution overcomes this constraint by enabling the multi-modal particle filter to estimate multiple trajectories for each object. The proposed filter is then tested in a challenging multi-object tracking scenario involving objects that can merge and separate. The results demonstrate that our approach yields superior tracking performance compared to the initial study and other relevant methods in the literature.

The increasing presence of power converters in large power systems has led to a growing number of oscillatory modes, which are now difficult to analyze using traditional methods. To address this issue, a new criterion for assessing the stability of power systems with a high number of oscillatory modes is proposed. This criterion is based on the concept of the distance to the nearest singularity and can be applied to power systems with a quadratic state matrix. The proposed criterion is verified using a case study of a 118-bus system with 100 wind turbines, where the proposed method is used to evaluate the stability of the system under different operating conditions.

The effectiveness of signature verification systems heavily relies on the distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of input templates. This paper introduces a new, two-stage signature forgery detection system that leverages the unique characteristics of these factors. In the initial stage, the system identifies and isolates the most distinctive and complex regions of a given signature using a convolutional neural network-based re-ranking mechanism. Subsequently, the system employs a support vector machine-based classifier to distinguish between genuine and forged signatures based on the extracted features. Experimental results conducted using two publicly available datasets demonstrate that this proposed system outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

We demonstrate that Hardy sums can be viewed as the sum of an oriented geodesic, which in turn leads to the discovery of an interpretation of the Dirichlet series associated with the Grossencharacter of the elliptic curve y^2=x^3-kx, and reveal a connection between its functional equation and the invariance of the measure of the geodesic flow, all achieved through the lens of arithmetic geometry on a specific elliptic curve.

Mobile app developers are increasingly incorporating context-awareness to tailor their applications to users' specific needs and preferences. This involves analyzing various environmental factors, such as location, time, and device type, to provide a personalized user experience. However, accurately identifying and utilizing context can be challenging due to the dynamic nature of these factors. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that employs a Bayesian network to model the relationships between context elements, enabling the detection of persistent contextual values. This method allows for the efficient identification of context that remains constant over time, facilitating the development of more effective context-aware mobile applications.

This study introduces a cutting-edge architecture for estimating the pose of a 3D object from a single image. The architecture is built around a 3D convolutional neural network, which is specifically designed to process volumetric data. The architecture incorporates a unique approach to processing 3D data, which involves breaking down the problem into smaller, more manageable parts. The architecture is tested on a variety of datasets, including a large-scale dataset of 3D objects, and achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of accuracy and speed. The results show that the architecture is able to estimate the pose of a 3D object in real-time, which is a significant improvement over previous methods. The architecture is also able to handle a wide range of objects, including complex shapes and textures. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of 3D convolutional neural networks for solving complex pose estimation problems.

Astronomers have found that AstroSat's AstroSat-LSI operates within its design parameters, but its 100 arcsec collimation is inaccurate. This issue has been addressed by recalculating the instrument's point spread function, which has enabled a more accurate assessment of the flux from various astronomical sources. This recalculated model has been used to measure the flux from a selection of gamma-ray sources, including AGNs, pulsars, and SNRs, with the results showing that the measurements are reliable for a subset of these sources. Specifically, the flux from a set of bright AGNs and pulsars has been accurately measured, while the flux from a set of SNRs has been found to be inaccurate. This discrepancy is likely due to the instrument's inability to accurately measure the flux from extended sources, which is a limitation of the AstroSat-LSI's design.

This research introduces a classification framework for blockchain protocols, enabling systematic analysis of their fundamental characteristics. By categorizing protocols as either permissioned or permissionless, and further examining the extent of their permissioned nature, and then evaluating the extent of user autonomy in the permissioning process, the framework provides a structured approach to understanding the differences between various blockchain systems. The research also delves into the underlying assumptions of the classification framework and explores its implications for the development of new blockchain protocols.

The model effectively accounts for the masses of the $\bar{D}D$, $\bar{D}^*D^*$, $\bar{D}D^*$, and $\bar{D}^*D$ meson pairs. It is found that the masses of the $\bar{D}D$ and $\bar{D}^*D$ meson pairs are lower than those of the $\bar{D}^*D^*$. The $X(3872)$ is found to be a $\bar{D}D$ molecular state, and the $X(3825)$ is found to be a $\bar{D}D$ molecular state with a lower excitation. In a modified version of the Standard Model, we examine the interplay between the Higgs mass and the scale of instability, particularly in light of recent advancements in our understanding of the theory. We find that incorporating the scale of instability into the analysis tightens the constraints on the Higgs mass, thereby reducing the likelihood of the theory's naturalness. Additionally, we investigate the implications of incorporating the axion as a singlet field, which can interact with the Higgs through a specific coupling. We find that this interaction can lead to a reduction in the Higgs mass, thereby relaxing the constraints on the theory's naturalness. We also explore the possibility of the axion field triggering a first-order phase transition, which can lead to the formation of gravitational waves. We find that the axion field can trigger a phase transition, which can lead to the formation of gravitational waves.

We establish the connection between the Talagrand inequality and its variant, specifically the $p$-Talagrand inequality, in Carnot groups through the use of Hamilton-Jacobi equation and $p-$gradient flow. This approach enables the derivation of the $p$-Talagrand inequality in specific cases, including He groups, under the condition of Ricci-Bernstein curvature, for $1 < p \le 2$.

This study introduces a novel estimator, known as the exponentially weighted divergence (EWD) estimator, which is founded on a weighted combination of divergence measures from the exponentially weighted average family. Building upon existing estimators such as the density power divergence (DPD) estimator, EWD incorporates robustness and enhanced efficiency. Key findings include the derivation of the asymptotic distribution of EWD, which is subsequently employed to construct confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. Empirical evidence from both simulation and real-world data analysis indicates that EWD outperforms DPD in terms of robustness and efficiency.

This paper introduces a new algorithm for image motion estimation, which leverages the concept of motion-centric and static-centric pixels. The algorithm's performance surpasses that of the Lucas-Kanade method, and it also outperforms the FlowNet 2.0 deep learning model in terms of accuracy.

This research examines the statistical properties of the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial for a specific class of random matrices, specifically those with symplectic properties, and their relationship to the underlying spectral zeta function. The study reveals that the variance of the coefficients is influenced by self-intersecting periodic orbits, and the research provides a quantitative measure of the effect of these intersections on the coefficients. The findings are supported by numerical simulations and the study also explores the relationship between the coefficients and the periods of the underlying periodic orbits.

This study presents a comprehensive catalog of 1,000 variable stars in the Milky Way's bulge, utilizing data from the Gaia DR2 mission. The catalog encompasses 1,000 stars, including 600 eclipsing binaries and 400 nebulous variables, identified through a rigorous examination of their light curves. The analysis involved the application of the Gaussian Mixture Model to categorize the stars, followed by the application of the Support Vector Machine for further classification refinement. The catalog provides detailed information on the stars, including their periods, light curve characteristics, and radial velocities, allowing for the identification of eclipsing binaries and nebulous variables. The study also highlights the presence of specific types of eclipsing binaries, such as Algol-type binaries, and nebulous variables, including Cepheids and RR Lyrae stars. The catalog provides a valuable resource for future research on variable stars in the Milky Way's bulge.

This research investigates the method of determining the nearest negative imaginary system from a given non-negative imaginary system in linear time invariant systems. A novel approach is presented to solve this problem, and it is demonstrated that the negative imaginary system with the smallest possible norm difference can be achieved by applying a negative sign to the positive imaginary components of the original system.

This study investigates the effectiveness of continual learning in End-to-End
Automatic Speech Recognition. We apply a widely used speech recognition model,
SeamlessMamba, to a series of 10 progressively difficult tasks, and compare its
performance to that of the standard fine-tuning approach. Our results indicate that
the most effective continual learning method surpasses fine-tuning by a margin of
up to 10% on a word error rate basis, and by as much as 10 percentage points in
character error rate. Furthermore, we observe that the performance of the
continual learning method is comparable to that of fine-tuning when dealing with
easier tasks, and that the standard fine-tuning method is more effective for
transcript recognition than the continual learning method.

The widespread use of code-switching in social media messages has made it difficult to accurately determine sentiment. To address this issue, we have developed a sentiment analysis model that utilizes the latest advancements in transformer-based language models. Our model incorporates two key components: a transformer-based code-switching classifier and a transformer-based sentiment classifier. The code-switching classifier identifies the language used in each part of a sentence, while the sentiment classifier determines the overall sentiment of the message. By combining these components, we have achieved a high level of accuracy in our sentiment analysis model, which outperforms existing methods in multiple languages. Our model also demonstrates its effectiveness in various scenarios, including multilingual settings, code-switching, and zero-shot learning.

A recent study revealed a possible particle candidate at the LHC with a mass of 90 GeV. This discovery prompted an investigation into a theoretical model known as the three-loop seesaw model, which predicts a lighter particle than a similar model. By analyzing the relationship between particle masses and coupling strengths, researchers found that the three-loop model can accommodate a particle with a mass of 90 GeV, with a corresponding mass of approximately 3.24 TeV for another particle. This result suggests that the three-loop model can be tested at the LHC, particularly in certain types of particle decay events.

The Product-based Neural Network (PNN) is a widely used algorithm for predicting interactions between categorical data fields. Its architecture is built around factorization machines, which are parameterized as a series of dot products between feature embeddings. This study delves into the relationship between PNNs and factorization machines, and investigates the effect of PNNs on feature importance. We derive a formula for the gradient of a factorization machine's loss function and propose a new method for calculating feature importance. Our method is demonstrated through a series of experiments on real-world datasets, and the results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and feature importance.

This research examines the challenge of designing active beamforming for a network utilizing intelligent reflecting surfaces, where the system lacks precise channel state information. To address this, we employ a robust optimization approach, maximizing the minimum signal-to-noise ratio across all users. By applying the S-procedure, we transform the problem into a series of solvable convex optimization problems. Subsequently, we introduce an innovative alternating optimization algorithm that combines this solution with a method for adjusting the phase of the IRS. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional designs that disregard phase adjustments at the IRS.

In the realm of branch prediction, researchers have long employed deep learning algorithms to create dynamic predictors that excel in forecasting branch behavior. However, these predictors often struggle to accurately predict branches that exhibit a high degree of variability. In response, we have developed a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both static and dynamic prediction methods. Our approach involves classifying branches as either predictable or unpredictable based on a set of predefined criteria, and then applying a deep learning-based dynamic predictor to the former, while utilizing a static method for the latter. By employing a novel metric called the branch entropy score, we have been able to effectively differentiate between predictable and unpredictable branches, and our results demonstrate that our hybrid approach outperforms existing static and dynamic prediction methods in terms of accuracy.

This study introduces a cutting-edge camera control system that combines a deep convolutional neural network and a reinforcement learning approach. The proposed system is designed to efficiently track and monitor targets in real-time, even in complex environments with multiple targets. By integrating a deep learning-based target detection and recognition module, the system can quickly identify and prioritize targets of interest. The reinforcement learning approach enables the system to optimize camera control and target monitoring in real-time, adapting to changing environmental conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of this system compared to traditional methods, showcasing its ability to achieve high tracking accuracy and efficient camera control.

We study the boundary laws of the SOS model on a lattice, focusing on its behavior on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and $T_d^d$. We find that the SOS model lacks normalizable boundary laws on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and has a unique normalizable boundary law on $T_d^d$. This outcome is a direct consequence of the SOS model's non-normalizable boundary laws.

We investigate the phenomenon of entangled two-photon resonance energy transfer (ETRP) in a system consisting of a donor and a acceptor, both with two-level systems. This process involves a two-photon entangled state, where one photon is absorbed by the donor and the other by the acceptor. A specific rate coefficient is used to characterize this ETRP process. Our study focuses on the effects of varying the strength of the donor-acceptor interaction and the donor-acceptor distance on this rate coefficient. Our findings indicate that the two-photon entangled state is particularly effective in facilitating E2P energy transfer under specific conditions, such as when the donor-acceptor interaction is strong and the donor-acceptor distance is short. Our research also reveals that the two-photon entangled state is more effective than a coherent two-photon state in facilitating E2P energy transfer.

The strong coupling constants of the $\eta_c$ and $J/\psi$ states are determined using the finite energy sum rules approach, which is applied to the corresponding decay processes. This method yields results that are in agreement with previous predictions made using other approaches.

Recent neutrino experiments have revealed consistent results from the T2K, MicroBoone, and MINOS+ studies. These findings are in line with neutrino data from the T2K and MicroBoone studies. A new analysis of the MINOS+ and NOvA studies also supports these results. A combined analysis of the T2K, MicroBoone, MINOS+, and NOvA studies reveals a significant deviation from the standard model, indicating a 3.2 sigma anomaly. A closer examination of the data reveals that the results are highly dependent on the neutrino parameters, particularly the value of the neutrino mass ordering. A more detailed analysis of the data reveals that the results are highly sensitive to the value of the neutrino parameters, particularly the value of the neutrino mass ordering.

Researchers have recently developed linear regression methods that assign weights to study participants based on how well they match a target population. These methods, which are designed to estimate causal effects, have been shown to be effective in observational studies. We investigate whether these methods can be used to improve observational study designs. We find that these methods can be used to determine the optimal sample size for observational studies, which can be used to minimize the variance of the estimated treatment effect. We also explore the potential of using these methods to design randomized trials, which can be used to estimate the precision of the treatment effect in a given population. We demonstrate the practical applications of these methods using simulated data and real-world datasets.

This study investigates the dynamic behavior of a grid-connected VSC-based DC power system, focusing on the effects of control parameters and grid interactions on oscillations. A multi-dimensional analysis is conducted to identify the key factors influencing the system's stability, and the results are used to develop a control strategy that can effectively mitigate oscillations. The proposed control algorithm utilizes the system's inherent dynamics to create a stable, low-amplitude oscillation-free operation. The effectiveness of the control strategy is verified through simulations and experiments, and the results demonstrate its potential to improve the overall stability and reliability of the DC power system.

We investigate the radiation patterns produced by a group of atoms in a cavity that emit photons due to quantum correlations. Our analysis shows that when two atoms decay, their emitted light exhibits quantum interference, but this effect disappears when three or more atoms decay, resulting in classically additive light. Our study also reveals that the light emitted when two or more atoms decay can be controlled by adjusting the system's parameters.

This study examines the stability of a kink in the $\phi^4$ theory, focusing on the impact of internal modes and the effect of varying the kink's width. The research shows that the internal mode can stabilize the kink, and a critical parameter value exists, beyond which the kink's position changes. The study also investigates the relationship between the kink's position and its position within the background, and finds that the kink's position can be influenced by its internal structure.

The study of hadron production in high-energy collisions is crucial for understanding generalized parton distributions (GPDs) and their underlying properties. This review focuses on hadron-production processes that can reveal GPDs and recent findings from experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. The review also highlights recent theoretical research on hadronization models and their impact on GPDs and related observables.

Neural networks are often trained with a single training set, but in reality, they are frequently tested on data from other datasets, which can be quite different. To address this issue, we've developed a new approach called DisNois, which is designed to improve the performance of neural networks on unseen test sets. Our method involves adding a controlled amount of random noise to the training data, which helps the model learn a decision boundary that is more robust to changes in the data distribution. We also introduce a technique called NoisErase, which smooths out the noisy data to prevent overfitting. Our results show that DisNois and NoisErase significantly improve the performance of neural networks on unseen test sets, even when the data from the test set is quite different from the training set.

Our research focuses on polyp detection in endoscopic procedures, a task that is often hindered by the limitations of existing methods. These methods typically fail to adequately capture the intricate details of polyps, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we introduce a novel channel-aware attention mechanism that enhances the representation of polyps by more effectively aggregating features. This mechanism is integrated into a two-stage framework, where the first stage generates a coarse prediction and the second stage refines it through localized analysis. The framework is further enhanced by a multi-task learning approach that simultaneously optimizes polyp detection and segmentation. The proposed method demonstrates exceptional performance on the Kvasir-V5 dataset, achieving a mean average precision of 91.1% and a Dice score of 0.89.

The variability can be controlled by a parameter ranging from 0 to 1, where 0 represents a standard sequential sampling method for a discrete uniform variable. The variable's expected value is denoted by the parameter. The proposed method is analogous to the continuous sampling method for the Beta distribution with parameters (a, 1-a). The method is shown to be efficient and efficient samples can be generated for a multivariate random variable with a Dirichlet distribution with a variability parameter. The method is applied to generate random variables with a multinomial distribution with a variability parameter. The method is applied to simulate the distribution of the number of times each nucleotide appears in a DNA sequence. We have developed a new set of nuclear reaction rates for the $rp$-process, which are based on a combination of theoretical and experimental data. This new network includes 108 nuclei and 2038 reactions, which we have used to model the $rp$-process in a Type-I X-ray burst. Our results show that a small fraction of the $rp$-process flow bypasses $^{56}$Ni, which is consistent with previous studies. We have also found that the production of $p$-process nuclei is sensitive to the initial composition of the burst, which we have modeled using a range of initial conditions. Our results suggest that the $p$-process nuclei produced in the burst are consistent with the observed abundances of the $p$-process nuclei in the Sun.

This article's main objective is to expand on the concept of flat cosets initially proposed by Drinfeld. We demonstrate that the flat components within this concept can be represented as torsion sets of an abelian scheme, whereas the non-flat components can be associated with translates of translation factors of the generalised Mumford domain. We then establish a direct correspondence between the flat components and subfields of a specific type of function field, and further show that the non-flat components correspond to translates of Mumford domain sections that are defined by a particular type of quadratic form. We also derive a criterion for determining when a given flat coset is dense within a specific type of algebraic variety.

Recent high-energy gamma-ray observations have significantly enhanced our understanding of the origins of gamma-ray emission in our galaxy. Observations from the Fermi-LAT, H.E.S.S., MAGIC, and other instruments have shed light on the nature of galactic gamma-ray sources, particularly those associated with pulsars and their surroundings. These findings have led to the development of new models for the galactic diffuse emission, which is a composite of radiation from various cosmic accelerators. Notably, the gamma-ray emission from pulsars and their environments has been a focal point of research, with recent observations of the Crab Nebula and its pulsar providing significant insights. Furthermore, the gamma-ray emission from dark matter has been a subject of investigation, with recent data from the Fermi-LAT and H.E.S.S. telescopes offering new constraints on the mass and annihilation cross-section of dark matter particles. Overall, the gamma-ray observations have provided valuable information about the nature of cosmic accelerators and the origins of cosmic rays.

This research examines the impact of nonlocal boundary conditions on the geometric structure of diffusion models. We investigate how the domain's geometry affects the diffusion process and demonstrate that the resulting energy functional is influenced by the domain's geometry. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations that illustrate the role of the domain's geometry in the diffusion process.

We have developed a novel method for categorizing compact stellar systems using the Galaxy Zoo 2 database, which contains images of these systems annotated by volunteers. Our approach involves analyzing the color of these systems to determine their type, and we have successfully trained a machine learning model to classify them into four distinct categories: globular clusters, dwarf spheroidal galaxies, dwarf spheroidal galaxies with active galactic nuclei, and dwarf spheroidal galaxies with active galactic nuclei. Our model has been trained using a combination of color features and has been found to be highly accurate, with a success rate of 80% on a test dataset. We have also discovered that the color of these systems is a strong indicator of their type, and we have used this information to create a more accurate classification system. Our results have significant implications for understanding the nature of compact stellar systems, and we hope that our method can be used to improve the accuracy of classifications in the Galaxy Zoo 2 database.

Recommender systems are complex systems that require careful design and development. To improve their construction process, we propose using simulations as a means to evaluate and compare different system designs. By creating a simulation model that mimics the behavior of a real recommender system, we can test and refine various approaches without the need for actual user interaction. This paper presents a simulation model that incorporates key components of a real-world recommender system, including a dataset, a ranking algorithm, and a set of evaluation metrics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this simulation model by using it to compare and analyze the performance of multiple ranking algorithms on a large dataset. Our results show that the simulation model provides accurate and reliable insights into the behavior of real-world recommender systems, and can be used to inform the design and development of new systems.

This study explores the statistical properties of truncated sample means, which are derived from trimming extreme values from a dataset. These means can be used to test hypotheses about distributional characteristics, such as heavy-tailed distributions with infinite mean or variance. By establishing the consistency of truncated sample means, the research enables the development of a novel test for examining heavy-tailed distributions. Additionally, the study demonstrates the asymptotic normality of truncated sample means, which facilitates the construction of confidence intervals. These findings are illustrated through simulations and a real-world application.

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) utilize EEG data to develop systems that can control external devices through a person's brain activity.  Deep learning models, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have been widely used in this field due to their ability to extract relevant features from data.  However, these models are often opaque and their internal workings are difficult to understand.  To address this limitation, researchers have turned to Explainable AI (XAI) to provide insight into the decision-making processes of these models.  This paper provides a comprehensive review of XAI methods applied to EEG data analysis in BCI systems.  It begins by explaining the fundamental concepts of XAI and then outlines the challenges associated with using EEG data.  Next, it discusses the various XAI methods used in EEG analysis and evaluates their performance.  Finally, it highlights the key findings and identifies areas for future research in this field.

The application of the $AdS/CFT$ correspondence to massive scalar fields in a noncommutative plane is explored, with the Kaluza-Klein reduction of a five-dimensional scalar field serving as a starting point. This approach generates noncommutative scalar fields in a four-dimensional theory, with the $AdS/CFT$ correspondence allowing for the identification of a dual CFT. The resulting correspondence reveals a relationship between the two-point functions of the deformed current and the $AdS_5$ scalar field, with the result being independent of the specific form of the noncommutative deformation matrix.

The allocation of kidney transplants has been a long-standing issue in the healthcare field.  Although there has been a significant amount of research on this topic, the existing models have limitations, particularly in their inability to account for the incompatibility state and the dynamic nature of the decision-making process.  This study aims to address these shortcomings by developing a new Markov Decision Process model that incorporates incompatibility as a dynamic state variable.  This model is then used to investigate the optimal acceptance policy, which is found to be a threshold-based policy.  Furthermore, the model is used to examine the effect of the waiting list on the optimal acceptance policy, revealing that the optimal policy is not necessarily monotonic in the waiting list size.  This finding has important implications for the healthcare system, as it suggests that there may be a trade-off between the number of transplants and the quality of the transplants.  This study also provides a new perspective on the problem of kidney transplantation, which can be used to inform future research and policy decisions.

This study compares the internal workings of Hidden Markov Models and Long Short-Term Memory Models by examining their hidden state representations. We discovered that these models store information in a similar manner, and their capacity to do so is constrained by the number of hidden states they possess. Furthermore, we found that the information stored in the hidden states is not static but rather decays over time, and this decay rate is influenced by the model's architecture. We also found that the information stored in the hidden states can be used to predict the next state of the model, and this prediction is more accurate than that of the model itself. These findings have important implications for the design of neural networks and the development of new algorithms for information storage and retrieval.

We investigate the conditions under which weighted Bergman space operators are compact or belong to the Schatten class. Our analysis focuses on integral operators with kernels that can be expressed as the sum of two functions, one of which is analytic in the inverse class and the other square-integrable.

To address the challenge of deploying large language models on resource-constrained devices, we investigate the effectiveness of various compressed architectures in text classification tasks. We experiment with three different compression methods: pruning, quantization, and pruning combined with low-precision quantization. We also introduce a new pruning technique called layer-wise pruning, which outperforms traditional pruning methods. Our experiments reveal that the compressed BERT model with low-precision quantization achieves the best balance between compression and performance. We also demonstrate that our pruning method can be applied to pre-trained models without compromising their performance.

This study focuses on matrix approximation techniques, particularly those that preserve certain matrix properties. The research also demonstrates how to derive the likelihood of a matrix being invertible or positive definite, and provides an approach to approximate the eigenvalues of a matrix that has been modified by these techniques.

The HTML and raw wikitext versions of Wikipedia articles are widely used for

To address this, we developed a method to identify the most relevant hyperlinks

navigating to it. Our approach was put to the test by comparing the relevance of

majority of these articles had a most relevant hyperlink in their HTML version.
Furthermore, we examined the relationship between the relevance of a hyperlink
and the content of the destination page, and we found a positive correlation
between the two.
